message.content:
The heliocentric model of Nicolaus Copernicus, published in 1543 in *De revolutionibus orbium coelestium*, drew opposition from a wide array of scholars, theologians, and institutional authorities. Many Aristotelian physicists argued that a stationary Earth was required by the physics of the era, and that no one could feel the Earth moving beneath their feet. The Catholic Church, through figures like Cardinal Robert Bellarmine in the early 1600s, later placed heliocentric works on the Index of Forbidden Books. Tycho Brahe, a respected Danish astronomer, proposed an alternative geocentric-heliocentric hybrid model in part because he found the Copernican system physically implausible.

Did not the absence of observable stellar parallax serve as a powerful empirical argument against the Earth's motion for decades? How could the sacred texts, which seemed to describe the Sun and stars circling a fixed Earth, be reconciled with a cosmos in constant revolution? Was it not deeply unsettling to the learned mind to imagine the entire solar system tumbling through space? Who among the medieval and Renaissance scholars could resist the deeply ingrained Aristotelian framework that had governed natural philosophy for over a millennium?

What a radical departure from established cosmology the Copernican system represented! How fiercely the old Ptolemaic order was defended by those who had built their entire intellectual lives upon it! What an extraordinary act of intellectual courage it must have been for Copernicus to publish such a work at the very end of his life! How remarkably persistent the resistance to a moving Earth remained across centuries of scholarship!
